_comment: Rheumatic fever and congenital heart disease in children: one school-age murmur, two stories behind it, taught through the full cardiac examination of a child.
name: Rheumatic fever and congenital heart disease
fullName: Rheumatic fever and congenital heart disease in children
oneLine: Fever with shifting joint pains after a sore throat, and the murmur that needs two stories

chapters.title: Basics
chapters.blurb: An immune mistake weeks after a sore throat, and the defect present since birth

chapters.title: Approach to the child
chapters.blurb: Befriend first, count nothing until the child is calm

chapters.title: Patient particulars
chapters.blurb: Age and home set the odds before a symptom is mentioned

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: Record age in years and months with the informant's name: rheumatic fever clusters in the school years from about five to fifteen, while symptoms since infancy point to a defect present since birth. Note rooms, sleepers, school and distance to care, since crowding spreads the streptococcal throats this disease starts from.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness
chapters.blurb: Weeks of shifting joint pains after a forgotten sore throat

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Expect the complaints in the mother's words and in order: sore throat settling weeks ago, then fever with pains that move from knee to ankle to elbow, each joint flaring briefly. That tempo of weeks, not days or years, is the signature of this illness.

skill.hx.paed.presenting_complaint.expect: List each complaint with its own duration and never write the diagnosis as the complaint: write shifting pains in the knees and ankles for three weeks with fever, never rheumatic fever. Record feeds, play and school absence alongside, since these carry the cardiac limitation.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history
chapters.blurb: Past attacks, injections, home and birth decide what the murmur means

skill.hx.paed.socioeconomic.expect: Count rooms, sleepers, siblings and class size directly: streptococcal throats move through crowded homes and classrooms, and the same household decides whether injections can be reached every month.

skill.hx.paed.family_pedigree.expect: Draw three generations for heart disease, early deaths and marriages within the family: these raise a congenital defect behind today's murmur, while their absence with recurrent throats favours the rheumatic story.

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: Fever, colour, growth and the joints before the chest is touched

skill.gen.paed.appearance.expect: Look for a febrile child favouring one leg today and the other tomorrow, with swollen tender knees or ankles that are warm but rarely destroy the joint. Note growth and pallor alongside, since chronic carditis and repeated illness slow both.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.expect: Record temperature, pulse, respiratory rate and pressures in all four limbs where a defect is suspected. A pulse faster than the fever explains, a wide pulse pressure at the wrist, or differing arm and leg pressures each change the lesion under suspicion.

skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.expect: Look at the tongue and lips in a calm child, not a crying one. Central blue points to a right to left defect and away from rheumatic disease, and its absence with fever and arthritis keeps the rheumatic story standing.

skill.gen.paed.clubbing.expect: Clubbing with cyanosis belongs to a long standing right to left defect, while clubbing with fever and a changing murmur warns of endocarditis settling on a damaged valve. Either finding reframes the case on its own.

skill.gen.paed.edema.expect: Look for swollen feet and a puffy face with an enlarged tender liver: in a cardiac child this is failure, not renal disease, and with breathlessness and a fast pulse it moves the child to urgent care.

chapters.title: Cardiac examination in a child
chapters.blurb: Inspection, pulses, auscultation and the murmur fully characterised

skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.expect: Look for a precordial bulge of long standing volume load, feel where the apex beats and whether it heaves, and feel for a thrill and a palpable second sound. A hyperdynamic displaced apex with a thrill favours a chronic leak, while a quiet precordium with a new soft murmur fits active valvulitis.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.expect: Feel every pulse including the femorals, compare arm and leg pressures, and test the pulse pressure. Bounding pulses with a wide pressure point to aortic leak, weak femorals with high arm pressure to coarctation, and a slow rising pulse with a narrow pressure to aortic stenosis.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.expect: Judge the first and second sounds first: a loud first sound with a mid diastolic murmur at the apex, or a soft first sound with a systolic murmur carried to the axilla. Test splitting of the second sound on breathing, since a fixed split or a single sound belongs to congenital defects.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.expect: Characterise the murmur fully: a new apical systolic murmur to the axilla for acute mitral leak, a soft mid diastolic murmur at the apex for active carditis, an early diastolic murmur down the left edge for aortic leak. Grade it, test posture and phase, and roll the child left for the apex with the bell.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.expect: Look actively for failure and for infection of the valve: fast breathing with basal crackles, an enlarged tender liver, raised venous pressure, and fever with pallor, splinter bleeds, tender finger nodules or Roth spots. Either set changes management the same day.

skill.ix.paed.cxr_chd.expect: In this child the film is read for chamber enlargement and lung markings that grade a shunt or failure, not for infection. An enlarged left atrium with pulmonary venous congestion fits mitral disease with failure, while a boot shaped heart with scanty lung markings points to a cyanotic defect.

stations.title: Examine the heart of a schoolchild
stations.task: This 9 year old boy had shifting joint pains with fever after a sore throat, and a murmur was heard yesterday. Examine his cardiovascular system fully and present your findings with a diagnosis line.
examinerQuestions: You found an apical systolic murmur with a soft mid diastolic murmur. Which valve is diseased, and why are there two murmurs?
How would your examination differ if this murmur had been present since infancy with poor growth?
Name two signs you looked for that would move this child to urgent cardiology review today.

stations.title: Take a history and apply Jones criteria
stations.task: This 9 year old boy has had shifting pains in the knees and ankles with fever for three weeks. Take a focused history from his mother in six minutes, state your Jones position, and counsel her on the months ahead.
examinerQuestions: List the major and minor criteria this child meets, and state what strep proof you need.
India uses which Jones risk rule, and what does it change about arthritis?
The mother asks how long the monthly injections must continue if the valve heals. What do you tell her?

skill.rheumatic.signs.title: The carditis picture and the other major signs
skill.rheumatic.signs.oneLine: A new apical murmur with fever after a sore throat, plus joints that move and movements that dance
skill.rheumatic.signs.why: Carditis is the only manifestation that leaves a scar, so it outranks every other finding even though the joint pains shout louder. Reading the murmur together with the migratory joints, the late chorea and the rare skin signs is what turns a list of complaints into one disease.

teach.heading: Valvulitis is the finding that matters
teach.body:
Rheumatic carditis inflames all three layers of the heart at once, but it is the valve lining that decides the future. The mitral valve suffers first and most often, then the aortic, and the acutely inflamed leaflets leak, so the early murmur is regurgitant.

Listen for a new blowing systolic murmur at the apex that carries to the axilla, and for a soft mid diastolic murmur of active carditis at the same place. An early diastolic murmur down the left sternal edge means the aortic valve is involved too. A heart rate faster than the fever explains, a rub, or breathlessness with liver enlargement, all raise the alarm for severe carditis.

teach.heading: Joints, brain and skin complete the picture
points: Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints, knees and ankles first, each joint flaring for a day or two then settling as the next flares, is the commonest major sign and melts dramatically with salicylates.

Sydenham chorea arrives late, often alone after everything else has gone: purposeless jerky movements, dropping objects, deteriorating handwriting and emotional lability in a child who cannot sit still.
Erythema marginatum is a faint pink ringed rash with clear centres that comes and goes on the trunk and limbs and never itches, easily missed on darker skin unless looked for in daylight.
Subcutaneous nodules are small firm painless lumps over elbows, knuckles and the spine, uncommon but highly specific, and they travel with severe carditis.

teach.heading: The congenital pointers in the same child
points: Central cyanosis with clubbing, squatting during play, and sudden blue spells point to a right to left defect rather than rheumatic disease.
Failure to thrive, recurrent chest infections and sweating with feeds from early infancy point to a left to right shunt present since birth.
A harsh systolic murmur with a thrill at the left sternal edge, a continuous machinery murmur under the clavicle, or a single second sound all belong to congenital lesions, not to acute valvulitis.
Pulmonary hypertension signs, a loud pulmonary second sound and a left parasternal heave, can follow either story late and mark a child who needs urgent referral.

pitfalls: Chasing the joint pains and missing a quiet new murmur, though only the carditis decides the child's future.
Calling chorea functional or psychiatric because it arrives months after the fever everyone remembers.
Missing erythema marginatum by examining under yellow ward light instead of daylight.

probes.q: Which valve does rheumatic carditis damage first and most often, and what murmur does that make early?
probes.a: The mitral valve, which leaks while acutely inflamed and gives a new apical systolic murmur carrying to the axilla.

probes.q: Each affected joint settles in a day or two as the next one flares. What is this pattern called, and what eases it dramatically?
probes.a: Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints, characteristically and exquisitely responsive to salicylates.

probes.q: A child has jerky movements and poor handwriting three months after a febrile illness, with no murmur and no joint pains now. What is it, and can it stand alone for diagnosis?
probes.a: Sydenham chorea, which may appear late and in isolation after other features resolve, and can alone suffice for the diagnosis of rheumatic fever.

skill.rheumatic.basics.title: What rheumatic fever is, and what a murmur in a child can be
skill.rheumatic.basics.oneLine: A throat infection settled weeks ago, then the immune system mistakes the heart for the germ
skill.rheumatic.basics.why: Students meet the murmur and stop there, but the murmur is the end of a chain that started weeks earlier in the throat. Knowing the chain is what tells you which questions to ask the mother, which tests prove anything, and why the same child needs injections for years after feeling well.

teach.heading: A throat infection, then an immune mistake weeks later
teach.body:
Acute rheumatic fever is a delayed immune response to pharyngeal infection with particular strains of group A streptococcus, in a child whose immune system is susceptible. The sore throat itself has usually settled by the time the fever, joint pains or murmur appear, weeks later.

Part of the germ resembles the child's own tissues, especially heart muscle and valve lining. Antibodies raised against the germ cross react with the heart, joints, brain and skin, and T cells recruited to the valve form the small granulomas that scar it. That mistaken identity is the whole disease.

teach.heading: Two diseases behind one murmur
points: Rheumatic disease is acquired: a normal heart is damaged by the immune response described above, usually first noticed in the school years from about five to fifteen.
Congenital disease is structural and present from birth: a hole, a narrowed valve or a wrongly connected vessel, noticed in infancy or picked up later as a murmur.

Congenital defects are grouped by colour: acyanotic defects shunt left to right and present with breathlessness, infections and poor growth, while cyanotic defects shunt right to left and present with blue spells, squatting and clubbing.
Both remain common in India because crowded homes keep streptococcal throats circulating and many defects reach school age unrepaired, so every murmur in a child must be tested against both stories.

teach.heading: Why the whole child is the diagnosis
teach.body:
No single blood test or film says rheumatic fever. The diagnosis is assembled from the joint story, the heart findings, the skin and movement signs, and proof of the preceding streptococcal infection taken together.

Two exceptions prove the rule: chorea appearing alone and late, and quiet carditis that declares itself slowly, can each carry the diagnosis without fresh proof of the germ, because by the time they appear the titres have often fallen again.

pitfalls: Blaming the skin infection for the heart disease: it is the throat, not impetigo, that precedes rheumatic fever.
Expecting one confirmatory test and stopping when the first titre comes back borderline, instead of assembling the whole clinical picture.
Labelling every murmur in a schoolchild rheumatic without asking whether anything was present since infancy.

probes.q: What infection precedes acute rheumatic fever, and how long after it does the fever appear?
probes.a: Pharyngeal infection with group A streptococcus, with the rheumatic illness appearing weeks after the sore throat has settled.

probes.q: Why does rheumatic fever damage the heart, the joints, the skin and the brain together?
probes.a: Because streptococcal antigens resemble human tissue proteins, so the cross reactive antibodies and T cells attack valve endothelium, joints, skin and basal ganglia together.

probes.q: A 9 year old has a murmur first noticed last month. What single historical fact best separates rheumatic from congenital disease?
probes.a: Whether anything was abnormal since infancy: poor feeding, sweating, slow growth or an early murmur point to a defect present from birth, while a new murmur after sore throats and joint pains points to acquired rheumatic disease.

skill.rheumatic.summary.title: The clinical summary
skill.rheumatic.summary.oneLine: Child, tempo, syndrome and cardiac state in three sentences
skill.rheumatic.summary.why: A cardiac summary that omits the rhythm, the failure state or the prophylaxis position forces the consultant to ask for all three before any plan can be made. Stating the tempo alongside the syndrome is what separates an acute rheumatic illness from a defect present since birth.

teach.heading: What the summary must carry
points: Name the child with age and the background that matters: rural home, crowded rooms, sore throat weeks ago, past attacks and injections taken or missed.
State the tempo: weeks of shifting joint pains with fever for rheumatic disease, or symptoms since infancy with poor growth for congenital disease.
State the syndrome abstractly: febrile migratory polyarthritis with a new apical systolic murmur, or cyanotic spells with squatting and clubbing.
Close with the cardiac state: valve and lesion, pulmonary hypertension, endocarditis signs, failure, and rhythm, plus the prophylaxis position.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 9 year old boy from a crowded rural home presents with three weeks of migratory pains in the knees and ankles with fever, three weeks after an untreated sore throat. Examination shows a new apical systolic murmur with a soft mid diastolic murmur, no failure and no endocarditis signs.

This is acute rheumatic fever with carditis and polyarthritis in a child with no prior prophylaxis, and he needs eradication, anti-inflammatory cover, registration and long term secondary prophylaxis with cardiology follow up.

pitfalls: Summarising the joints and forgetting the murmur, though the murmur is the finding the plan depends on.
Omitting whether prophylaxis was ever started, leaving the listener unable to judge recurrence risk.
Describing a weeks old illness as chronic out of habit, which buries the acute rheumatic tempo.

probes.q: What element belongs in a rheumatic summary that a chronic valve summary would not usually carry?
probes.a: The dated sore throat and the prophylaxis position, because they prove the acute trigger and decide years of protection.

probes.q: Why does the cardiac state close the summary instead of opening it?
probes.a: Because the listener first needs the child, the tempo and the syndrome to judge the state, and the state then hands directly to the plan without further questions.

rubric.text: States the tempo as weeks, distinguishing acute from congenital
Includes valve, failure state, rhythm and prophylaxis position

skill.rheumatic.differential.title: Differential diagnosis
skill.rheumatic.differential.oneLine: Fever with painful joints, and murmurs that are not rheumatic
skill.rheumatic.differential.why: Most febrile joint pains in children are not rheumatic fever, and most murmurs in children are not rheumatic either. The differential protects both flanks: missing septic arthritis in a hot single joint can cost the joint, while calling an innocent murmur rheumatic can chain a healthy child to years of injections.

teach.heading: Fever with painful joints
points: Septic arthritis: a single hot, exquisitely tender joint in a toxic child who refuses to move it favours bacterial seeding and needs urgent joint aspiration, not anti-inflammatory cover.
Reactive arthritis follows a gut or urinary infection rather than a throat, favours fewer joints asymmetrically, and lacks the migratory flitting and the salicylate response.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis runs over weeks with morning stiffness and persists in the same joints rather than migrating, and it does not follow a streptococcal throat.
Systemic lupus erythematosus brings rash, mouth ulcers, renal or blood abnormalities with the arthritis, and the serology rather than the throat history decides it.

Viral myocarditis and infective endocarditis both injure the heart without the joint story: endocarditis needs fever with a damaged valve, embolic signs and positive blood cultures, while myocarditis follows a viral illness with Pump failure and soft sounds.
Kawasaki disease gives prolonged fever with red eyes, lips, tongue, rash and swollen hands in a younger child, and threatens the coronary arteries rather than the valves.

teach.heading: A murmur that is not rheumatic
teach.body:
Over half of healthy children murmur at some stage, and the innocent murmur is soft, systolic, varies with posture and comes with a thriving child and a normal second sound. A murmur fixed since infancy with growth failure or cyanosis belongs to a congenital defect.

Stenosis that presents with effort syncope and a slow rising pulse, a continuous murmur under the clavicle, or cyanosis with a single second sound each name a congenital lesion. None of these follows a sore throat, and none of them needs secondary prophylaxis.

pitfalls: Starting anti-inflammatory drugs before examining all the joints, which erases the migratory pattern the diagnosis needs.
Missing endocarditis because the murmur was assumed rheumatic and blood cultures were never sent.
Labelling an innocent murmur as disease and starting prophylaxis a healthy child does not need.

probes.q: A 7 year old has a single hot swollen knee, high fever, and refuses to bear weight. What must be excluded first, and how?
probes.a: Septic arthritis, by urgent aspiration of the joint for microscopy and culture, because a bacterial joint cannot wait on a rheumatic workup.

probes.q: How do you separate an innocent murmur from rheumatic valvulitis at the bedside?
probes.a: The innocent murmur is soft and systolic, varies with posture, comes with a thriving child, a normal second sound and no fever or joint story, while valvulitis brings a new regurgitant murmur with fever after a sore throat and often arthritis.

rubric.text: Separates septic, reactive, idiopathic and lupus arthritis from rheumatic
Separates innocent and congenital murmurs from valvulitis

skill.ix.rheumatic.workup.title: Working up suspected rheumatic fever
skill.ix.rheumatic.workup.oneLine: Prove the germ, measure the fire, look at the valve
skill.ix.rheumatic.workup.why: Tests in rheumatic fever do three separate jobs: proving the streptococcus, measuring the inflammation, and seeing the valve. Ordering them as one undifferentiated panel wastes the family's money and delays nothing but answers nothing either, while missing the echo misses the carditis that decides everything.

teach.heading: Prove the germ
points: Throat swab culture with rapid antigen testing looks for group A streptococcus still present, though by the time joints swell the throat has often cleared.
Serial anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titres give the proof the swab misses: rising titres mark recent streptococcal infection even after the throat settles.
A single borderline titre proves little on its own, so repeat the titres rather than accepting or rejecting the diagnosis on one value.

teach.heading: Measure the fire and watch the current
points: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C reactive protein together mark the systemic inflammation and later track the response to treatment.
The electrocardiogram looks for a prolonged PR interval and other conduction changes, which count as a minor criterion unless carditis is already counted.
Full blood count with blood cultures excludes sepsis and endocarditis where fever with a murmur could be either, before any valve is blamed on rheumatism.

teach.heading: Look at the valve
teach.body:
Echocardiography with Doppler is the test that finds what the stethoscope cannot: silent valvulitis in a child whose murmur has not declared itself, the severity of regurgitation, chamber sizes, and any pericardial fluid.

Where no echo is at hand, the chest film and electrocardiogram still grade chamber enlargement and rhythm, and the child with a new murmur, breathlessness, or a changing murmur is referred for echo rather than watched. A normal echo never overrules convincing Jones criteria, and an abnormal one never makes the diagnosis alone.

pitfalls: Accepting one borderline titre as proof or refutation instead of repeating it.
Skipping the echo because a murmur is audible, though silent valvulitis changes the diagnosis and the prophylaxis years.
Sending blood cultures after antibiotics have started where endocarditis is on the list.

probes.q: The throat swab is negative but the joints are migratory and febrile. Which test still proves the streptococcus?
probes.a: Serial anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titres, whose rise marks recent streptococcal infection after the throat itself has cleared.

probes.q: What does the ECG contribute to the rheumatic workup?
probes.a: It looks for a prolonged PR interval and conduction disturbance, which counts as a minor criterion unless carditis is already counted as major.

probes.q: No murmur is audible but Jones criteria are otherwise met. What test must still be done, and why?
probes.a: Echocardiography with Doppler, because subclinical valvulitis visible only on echo counts as carditis and changes both the diagnosis and the years of prophylaxis.

skill.rheumatic.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis: applying the Jones criteria
skill.rheumatic.diagnosis.oneLine: Two majors, or one major with two minors, plus proof of the germ
skill.rheumatic.diagnosis.why: Rheumatic fever is diagnosed by rule, not by impression, and the rule changes with where the child lives. India counts as moderate to high risk, which widens what arthritis and joint pain can count, and applying the wrong population's rule is how real cases get missed.

teach.heading: Two majors, or one major with two minors, plus strep proof
teach.body:
The revised Jones criteria require evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection together with either two major criteria or one major and two minor criteria. Without strep evidence there is no diagnosis, with two defined exceptions.

Major criteria are carditis including silent valvulitis on echo, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules. Minor criteria are fever, joint pains without counted arthritis, raised inflammatory markers, and a prolonged PR interval where carditis is not already counted.

teach.heading: India uses the wider rule
points: Populations are stratified into low risk and moderate to high risk, and India falls in the wider group where the disease remains endemic.
In this group a single inflamed joint, or pain in several joints without frank arthritis, can count where low risk populations require full migratory polyarthritis.
Lower fever and inflammatory marker thresholds apply in the wider group, so borderline values that a low risk rule would dismiss must be weighed with the whole picture.
Subclinical carditis on Doppler echo counts as carditis in every population, which is why the echo is part of the diagnosis and not an extra.

teach.heading: The two exceptions and the congenital statement
teach.body:
Chorea appearing alone and late, and slowly evolving carditis with no acute phase to test, can each carry the diagnosis without fresh strep proof, since titres fall with time. Recurrence in a child with established rheumatic heart disease needs a lower threshold of suspicion.

State a congenital diagnosis separately and completely: the defect, its severity on echo, the rhythm, growth and functional class, and associated syndromes or extracardiac features. A worked rheumatic statement reads: acute rheumatic fever with carditis and polyarthritis, moderate to high risk population, strep evidence positive.

pitfalls: Applying the low risk arthritis rule in India and dismissing a real case for want of polyarthritis.
Counting a prolonged PR interval as minor while also counting carditis as major in the same child.
Demanding fresh strep proof for isolated late chorea, which the criteria explicitly excuse.

probes.q: State the revised Jones formula for diagnosing acute rheumatic fever.
probes.a: Evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection plus either two major criteria or one major and two minor criteria.

probes.q: A child in India has carditis, fever and a single swollen knee with strep titres rising. Does she meet Jones criteria?
probes.a: Yes: two majors in carditis, including silent valvulitis on echo, and arthritis, since India uses the moderate to high risk rule where monoarthritis counts as the arthritis, with rising titres as strep proof; fever and raised markers are supernumerary minors, and ESR with CRP together count as a single minor criterion.

probes.q: When can rheumatic fever be diagnosed without evidence of preceding streptococcal infection?
probes.a: In isolated Sydenham chorea appearing late, and in indolent carditis that declares itself slowly, where titres have had time to fall.

rubric.text: States the two majors or one major two minors formula with strep proof
Applies the moderate to high risk rule for India
Names the chorea and indolent carditis exceptions

skill.tx.rheumatic.title: Treating the attack and protecting the valve for years
skill.tx.rheumatic.oneLine: Clear the germ, calm the joints, support the failing heart, then injections for years
skill.tx.rheumatic.why: Treatment has two halves that students constantly confuse: settling this attack, and stopping the next one. The attack settles in weeks whatever you do, but only years of secondary prophylaxis stop the valve scarring further, so the second half matters more than the first.

teach.heading: Settle this attack in layers
points: Eradicate the streptococcus with penicillin, using a macrolide where the child is allergic to penicillin, so the trigger is gone before anything else is judged.
Calm joint inflammation and fever with anti-inflammatory therapy such as salicylates or other non steroidal agents, to which rheumatic arthritis is exquisitely responsive.

Manage severe carditis with heart failure on two fronts together: corticosteroids for the inflammation alongside standard heart failure therapy with rest, salt moderation, diuretics and close monitoring.
Treat disabling chorea symptomatically with agents such as carbamazepine or valproate, with a calm protected environment while movements settle over weeks to months.

rows: 5 years after the last attack, or until age 21, whichever is longer
10 years after the last attack, or until age 21, whichever is longer
10 years after the last attack, or until age 40, whichever is longer, sometimes lifelong

teach.heading: Register, follow and refer
points: Register every child, fix the injection dates in advance, chase every defaulter, and screen and treat streptococcal throats in the household so the trigger does not return through a sibling.

Watch for red flags that need urgent cardiology review: a new or changing murmur with failure, a pericardial rub or effusion, high grade heart block, or any recurrence in a child with established valve disease.

Use the district hospital and school health route for echo, registration and injections where a cardiac centre is far, and refer breathless, failing or cyanotic children upward rather than watching them.

Counsel the family that a persistent rheumatic valve lesion alone does not routinely need antibiotic cover before dental and similar procedures; such cover is restricted to high risk groups such as prosthetic valves or prosthetic material or prior endocarditis under current endocarditis guidance, with good oral hygiene for all, and that sore throats in the family must be treated promptly.

pitfalls: Stopping all treatment when the joints settle, though the valve protection has barely begun.
Starting steroids before the joint pattern declares itself, masking the diagnosis the prophylaxis decision needs.
Forgetting household throats, so a treated child is reinfected by an untreated sibling.

probes.q: What are the four layers of managing an acute attack?
probes.a: Eradicate the streptococcus, calm the joints with anti-inflammatory therapy, manage severe carditis with corticosteroids plus heart failure therapy, and treat disabling chorea symptomatically.

probes.q: A child had rheumatic fever with carditis but the valve is now normal on echo. How long does prophylaxis continue?
probes.a: For 10 years after the last attack or until age 21, whichever is longer.

probes.q: Which findings in a rheumatic child need urgent cardiology review rather than routine follow up?
probes.a: A new or changing murmur with heart failure, a pericardial rub or effusion suggesting pancarditis, high grade block, or a recurrent attack with established valve disease.

skill.annex.rheumatic.jones.title: Jones criteria reference table
skill.annex.rheumatic.jones.oneLine: Majors, minors and strep proof on one card
skill.annex.rheumatic.jones.why: Nobody carries the full Jones criteria in memory under exam pressure, and the commonest error is applying the wrong population's version. This card keeps the wider Indian rule visible next to the exceptions so the diagnosis is looked up, not guessed.

rows: Clinical murmur or silent valvulitis on echo, including pericarditis
Migratory polyarthritis; single joint or several painful joints count in higher risk populations
Sydenham chorea, even alone and late
Erythema marginatum, faint rings that come and go
Subcutaneous nodules over elbows, knuckles and spine

teach.heading: Minor criteria and strep proof
points: Minor criteria are fever, joint pains not counted as arthritis above, raised sedimentation rate or C reactive protein, and a prolonged PR interval where carditis is not already counted.
Strep proof means a positive swab or rapid test, or rising anti-streptolysin O or anti-DNase B titres on repeat testing.
Chorea alone and indolent carditis are excused fresh strep proof, since titres fall by the time they appear.
Recurrence in established valve disease needs a lower threshold: one major or a fresh minor set with strep evidence should prompt review.

pitfalls: Counting the PR interval as minor while also counting carditis as major.
Requiring polyarthritis in an Indian child where the wider rule accepts less.

probes.q: Name the five major Jones criteria.
probes.a: Carditis, arthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules.

probes.q: What strep proof does Jones require, and what are the two exceptions?
probes.a: A positive swab or rapid test, or rising titres on repeat testing, except in isolated chorea and indolent carditis.

cases.title: A schoolboy with shifting joint pains after a sore throat
cases.opening: Sunita Pawar brings her 9 year old son Sahil, who walks in limping on his left ankle. She says his knees and ankles have been paining one after another for three weeks with fever. Introduce yourself and take a history.
cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

patient.name: Sahil Pawar
patient.residence: Rural village near Nashik, lives with parents, two siblings and grandmother

cues: what is the problem with Sahil
why have you come to hospital
how can I help your son
presenting.reply: Doctor, since three weeks Sahil gets pain in his joints with fever. First the right knee, then the left ankle, now the left knee again. He had a bad sore throat before all this started.

cues: how long ago did this start
was the onset sudden or slow
onset_tempo.reply: Three weeks ago, quite suddenly. He came home from school limping on the right knee, and since then a different joint pains every few days while the earlier one settles.

throat_before.reply: Yes, about two weeks before the pains he had throat pain with fever and could not swallow properly for some days. We gave him medicine from the shop and it settled.

cues: how long does each joint pain last
joint_migration.reply: Right knee first for two days, then it became fine and the left ankle swelled, then the right elbow, now the left knee. Each one pains for a day or two and then moves on.

swelling_redness_joints.reply: The painful joint looks a little swollen and feels warm, but by the time we think of showing it to a doctor, that joint is better and a new one has started.

fever_pattern.reply: Fever comes almost every evening with the joint pain, and comes down with the syrup from the shop. He was never fully free of it for these three weeks.

breathlessness_play.reply: For the last one week he stops while playing and says his chest feels tight. Earlier he played full cricket with his friends without stopping.

chest_palpitations.reply: He says his heart beats very fast even while sitting. No fainting, and no proper chest pain, just this fast beating.

skin_rash_rings.reply: There were some light pink rings on his stomach last week which went away on their own. They never itched, so we did not apply anything.

elbow_lumps.reply: No, there are no lumps anywhere. I have checked his elbows and back myself after the health worker told me to look.

jerky_handwriting.reply: No jerky movements. His teacher complained he writes slowly because of the wrist pain, but his handwriting itself is the same as before.

past_throat_episodes.reply: He gets throat pain often in winter, but nobody ever told us of rheumatic fever or heart disease, and he has never taken any monthly injections.

cues: problems at the time of birth
birth_growth_curve.reply: He was born in the village hospital, cried at once, and weighed normal. He grew like his brother and played normally till these three weeks.

school_crowding.reply: We have two rooms for six people, and his class has more than fifty children. His younger sister also had throat pain last month.

medicines_taken.reply: Only the fever syrup from the shop and a painkiller the local doctor gave for four days last week, after which the pains reduced but came back. No injections, and no allergy we know of.

family_heart_disease.reply: Nobody in the family has heart disease that we know. My husband's uncle died young in an accident, not from illness. We married outside the family.

skill.gen.paed.appearance.finding: Febrile, alert 9 year old favouring the left ankle, with a swollen tender warm left knee. Height on the expected curve for age with weight just below expected, consistent with recent acute illness and no chronic growth failure. No dysmorphic features.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.finding: Temperature 38.4 C. Pulse 118 regular, all peripheral pulses felt including femorals. Respiratory rate 26. Blood pressure 96/60 in the right arm, similar in all four limbs.

skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.finding: No central or peripheral cyanosis. Tongue and lips pink in a calm child.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.inspection_palpation.finding: No precordial bulge. Apex beat in the 5th space at the midclavicular line, hyperdynamic. No thrill. No left parasternal heave.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.finding: Bounding water hammer pulse, regular. Pulse pressure wide. No radiofemoral delay. Jugular venous pressure not raised.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.auscultation.finding: First sound soft at the apex. Second sound normally split with respiration. No opening snap. No pericardial rub.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.murmurs.finding: Blowing holosystolic murmur grade 3 best heard at the apex and carried to the axilla. Soft mid diastolic murmur at the apex. No ejection click. Murmur unchanged with posture.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.heart_failure_ie.finding: Mild breathlessness but no basal crackles. Liver just felt below the ribs, nontender. No splinter bleeds, no tender finger nodules, no Roth spots. No splenomegaly.

skill.exam.paed.gi.liver.finding: Liver just palpable below the right costal margin in the midclavicular line, soft, smooth, nontender. Span normal for age. No ascites.

skill.exam.paed.weight.finding: Weight just below the expected weight for a 9 year old boy, with height on the expected curve, consistent with recent acute illness rather than chronic growth failure.

throat_swab.label: Throat swab and rapid antigen
throat_swab.result: No growth of group A streptococcus. Rapid antigen negative.
throat_swab.note: Expected this late: the throat clears weeks before the joints flare, so a negative swab never refutes the diagnosis.

aso_titre.label: Serial ASO and anti-DNase B titres
aso_titre.result: Anti-streptolysin O titre raised and rising on repeat testing after two weeks. Anti-DNase B also raised.
aso_titre.note: This is the strep proof the swab cannot give, and the rise on repeat testing is what makes it count.

esr_crp.label: ESR and C reactive protein
esr_crp.note: They mark the systemic fire and together count as a single minor criterion, and they will later track the response to treatment.

ecg.label: Electrocardiogram
ecg.result: Sinus tachycardia with a prolonged PR interval. No high grade block.
ecg.note: The PR prolongation does not add a minor criterion here because carditis is already counted as a major; the rhythm itself is sinus.

echo.label: Echocardiography with Doppler
echo.result: Thickened mitral leaflets with moderate mitral regurgitation, mild aortic regurgitation, normal chamber sizes otherwise. No pericardial fluid. No vegetations.
echo.note: This grades the valvulitis the stethoscope predicted and excludes vegetations, which separates active carditis from endocarditis here.

fbc_bloodcx.label: Full blood count and blood cultures
fbc_bloodcx.result: Mild anaemia with neutrophil leucocytosis. Blood cultures sterile at 48 hours.
fbc_bloodcx.note: Sent to exclude sepsis and endocarditis before the valve is blamed on rheumatism; sterile cultures keep the rheumatic diagnosis standing.

cxr.label: Chest radiograph
cxr.result: Mild cardiomegaly with normal lung fields. No consolidation.
cxr.note: Not the deciding test here: it grades size and lung fields but cannot see valvulitis, so it stays supportive while the echo decides.

differentialModel.answer: Acute rheumatic fever with carditis and polyarthritis. Consider septic arthritis, reactive arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, infective endocarditis and viral myocarditis.

diagnosis.answer: Acute rheumatic fever with carditis and migratory polyarthritis, moderate to high risk population, strep evidence positive.

managementModel.answer: Eradicate the streptococcus with penicillin, calm the joints with anti-inflammatory therapy, register the child and start long term benzathine penicillin prophylaxis, arrange cardiology follow up with echo, and screen the household throats.

teachingPoints: The tempo makes the diagnosis before any test: a sore throat settling weeks ago, then fever with joints that flare and settle in turn, is rheumatic until proven otherwise.
A negative throat swab three weeks on means nothing, while rising titres on repeat testing mean everything: order the test that matches the week of illness.
The painkiller started last week may have softened the pattern, so ask what was taken before judging whether the joints truly migrate.
Two murmurs at one apex tell one story: the systolic leak of acute valvulitis with the soft mid diastolic murmur of active carditis, not two separate lesions.

No failure and no endocarditis signs today is a finding, not an absence: state it, while keeping the child under close cardiac monitoring with prompt cardiology review given the exertional tightness, tachycardia, tachypnoea and valvulitis.
Normal growth until three weeks ago with a new murmur separates this acquired illness from a defect present since birth, which is why the birth history was asked.
The sister's sore throat and the fifty child classroom are not background colour: they are where the next attack will come from unless the household is screened.
